title: News, Research & Insights
author: Sean Harris
summary: This is Sean Harris's weekly roundup (w/c 2 November 2026) on poverty, place and education from Tees Valley Education, pairing five news headlines with four commentated research items and a short opportunities section. The news covers the Children's Commissioner's postcode analysis, 100,000 hospitality placements for 18 to 24 year olds, health professionals urging caution over classroom screen time, a JRF projection of falling incomes for the poorest fifth, and an eye-gaze user passing seven GCSEs. The research items are Harris's own Sutton Trust piece on resisting deficit narratives, the Children's Commissioner's Childhood Lottery report in which Middlesbrough scores lowest in England at 408 out of 960, an EEF blog on seeing the learner for inclusive teaching, and his 2024 Blockbuster Effect post. Each carries a My takeaway note, with a recurring theme that educators should ask what needs to change around children rather than what is wrong with them. The opportunities section lists Marc Rowland's free resources, the SHINE Let Teachers SHINE grants and a December poverty-informed practice event. The Sutton Trust piece and the EEF blog were expanded as separate entries.
points: Harris argues that educators must resist deficit narratives, since a community can have high child poverty and also assets, industries and expertise worth connecting young people to.

The Children's Commissioner's Childhood Lottery report scores local authorities on 162 measures of childhood, with Middlesbrough lowest in England and the report urging a Children's Test for devolution.
Harris frames the Middlesbrough finding as a question about what needs to change around children, not what is wrong with them.
The EEF blog on seeing the learner is summarised as saying labels should inform professional judgement rather than replace it, with checking for understanding guiding adaptations.
The roundup closes with practical opportunities, including free resources from Marc Rowland and teacher-led innovation grants up to 25,000 pounds from SHINE.
quotes: We need to be very careful about explaining educational inequality through supposed deficits in children, families or communities.
A place can experience significant child poverty while simultaneously having assets, industries, expertise and opportunities worth celebrating and connecting young people to.

Poverty changes the conditions in which opportunity is encountered. That is why talking simply about raising aspiration can be problematic. It places attention on changing the young person when we might need to change the conditions around the opportunity instead.
Middlesbrough receives the lowest overall score in England (408 out of 960). The next lowest, Hounslow, scores 460.
The finding should not lead us to ask: “What is wrong with children in Middlesbrough?” but rather “what needs to change around children in Middlesbrough?

A pupil experiencing disadvantage may understand something immediately, while another pupil without an obvious additional need may require explicit teaching or modelling. Labels should therefore inform professional judgement rather than replace it
Labels can help us understand potential barriers, but they should never become a substitute for understanding the child.

There is a useful leadership angle too. Schools can give teachers opportunities to discuss pupils, challenge assumptions and explore whether adaptations are genuinely helping learning rather than unintentionally creating dependence.
